title: 3-D objects
status: draft: written 13 Nov 2026 from research round 3; shorter entries; not yet checked by a Kenyan maths teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Use objects every Kenyan child knows: a dice, a matchbox, a tin of Kimbo or cooking fat, a football, a round hut roof (a cone, not a pyramid). Show objects turned and in different sizes, because children recognise shapes only in their usual position.

skills.key_step: The child names cubes, cuboids, cylinders, spheres and pyramids by their features, whatever their size, material or position.

floor.prerequisite: Names flat shapes (square, rectangle, circle, triangle).
floor.question: What flat shape is the face of a dice?

steps: Sort real objects into groups by shape.
Turn objects: a tin on its side, a pyramid on its point.
Compare a cube (all faces square) with a cuboid.

board.do: Draw a tin standing, then the same tin lying on its side.
Ask whether the lying tin is still the same shape.
board.say: Is it still the same shape?

board.do: Wait for the child to name it and say why.

misconceptions.ask: Are all the faces of a brick the same square?
misconceptions.repair: A cube has six equal square faces; a box with rectangles is a cuboid.

listen_for: the hut roof is a pyramid
misconceptions.ask: Does the hut roof have flat triangle faces, or a curved surface?
misconceptions.repair: A pyramid has flat faces and a flat base with straight sides; a round roof is a cone.

misconceptions.ask: Stand the tin up again. Did its shape change?
misconceptions.repair: Turning an object does not change what it is.

misconceptions.ask: Do both have two flat circles and a curved side?
misconceptions.repair: Shape is about faces and surfaces, not size or material.

checks.question: Is a building brick a cube or a cuboid?
A tin of Kimbo is lying on its side. What 3-D object is it?

skills.key_step: The child describes surfaces (flat, curved, both), corners and edges, and whether an object rolls, slides or both.

floor.question: Name an object shaped like a ball.

steps: Count corners, including the base of a pyramid.

board.do: Draw a square-based pyramid; highlight the top point.
Child counts all corners, the board marking each.
board.say: Count every corner, top and bottom.

misconceptions.ask: Are there corners at the bottom too?
misconceptions.repair: Count the base corners as well: four plus the top.

misconceptions.ask: Can a tin stand on its end? What is that end like?
misconceptions.repair: A cylinder has two flat ends and one curved surface.

misconceptions.ask: Lay the tin on its side and push it. What happens?
misconceptions.repair: Anything with a curved surface can roll; a tin rolls on its side and slides on its end.

checks.question: How many corners does a square-based pyramid have?
Which can roll: a football, a tin of milk, a matchbox?

skills.key_step: The child uses flat-shape names for flat shapes and solid names for solid objects, and explains that any real object, however thin, is 3-D.

floor.question: What flat shape is a drawn circle?

steps: Put a ball beside a drawn circle.
Discuss a coin and a chapati: thin, but you can hold them, so 3-D.

board.do: Draw a flat circle beside a shaded ball.

misconceptions.ask: Can you hold a circle drawn on paper the way you hold an orange?
misconceptions.repair: A circle is flat; a ball shape you can hold is a sphere.

misconceptions.ask: Can you stack coins? Does a stack have height?
misconceptions.repair: Every coin has a little thickness, so it is 3-D (a very short cylinder).

skills.key_step: The child names the flat faces of each object, including hidden ones, and knows curved surfaces are not faces.

floor.question: Is the side of a tin flat or curved?

representations: tracing round faces of real objects
steps: Trace round each flat face of a box on paper.
Pyramid: triangles and a square base.
Cylinder: two circles; the curved side is not a face.

board.do: Draw a cube box; unfold it slowly into its net, one face at a time.
Child counts the squares as they unfold.
Wait for the total and the shape name.

misconceptions.ask: What about the bottom and the back?
misconceptions.repair: Unfold the box: every face appears, hidden ones too.

misconceptions.ask: What does the pyramid stand on?
misconceptions.repair: Lift the pyramid in the drawing: the base is a square.

misconceptions.ask: Can a football stand flat on a table?
misconceptions.repair: A sphere has no flat face; its outline looks round but every part is curved.

misconceptions.ask: Is the side of the tin flat?
misconceptions.repair: The side is curved, so it is not a face; only the two circles are flat.

checks.question: Mwangi traces every face of a cube-shaped box. How many squares?
What flat shapes are found on a tin of Kimbo?
checks.shows: curved surface is not a face
